(1) the effects of known irrationality on reward learning are predictable, (2) the effects of unknown irrationality are unpredictable, and (3) the effects of both are small.
the effects of irrationality on reward learning depend on the demonstrator’s irrationality and the learning algorithm’s assumptions about it.
the effects of irrationality on reward and transition model inference are highly problem-dependent and that, for the problems we consider, the effects are often more severe than the effects of noise.

The impacts of known and known demonstrator irrationality is not known.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we find that the effects of demonstrator irrationality can be quite significant, and that modeling these irrationalities can improve reward inference.
, when the demonstrator is irrational, reward inference can be significantly improved by using a demonstrator model that accounts for the demonstrator's irrationality.
, when a demonstrator's irrationality is known, we can leverage this knowledge to improve reward inference.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the benefits of modeling demonstrator irrationality depend strongly on the nature of the demonstrator’s behavior, the nature of the task, the type of reward function, and the type of demonstrator irrationality.
irrationalities that cause demonstrator behavior to diverge from optimal behavior are detrimental to reward inference.
, while the impact of irrationality on inference is highly dependent on the particular form of irrationality considered, in general, irrationality is not necessarily a barrier for accurate inference.
